hints: Count the shared pairs of electrons in the overlap region of the dot-cross diagram for CO and recall the bonding in N2.
Look closely at the symbols in the shared region, dots versus crosses, to see which atom supplied both electrons for one of the pairs.
walkthrough:
Read what the dot-cross diagram is telling you**
Think of crosses as electrons from carbon and dots as electrons from oxygen. In the middle overlap you can see three pairs. That means three shared pairs in total, so carbon and oxygen are joined by a triple bond, exactly like the $\text{N}\equiv\text{N}$ triple bond.

Spot the odd one out in how the pairs formed**
In $\text{N}_{2}$ each nitrogen supplies one electron to each shared pair. In $\text{CO}$ look at the bottom pair in the overlap, it is shown as two dots only. Both electrons came from oxygen alone. When one atom provides both electrons for a shared pair, we call it a dative or coordinate bond. That is the key difference.

Final answer: Similarity: both $\text{CO}$ and $\text{N}_{2}$ contain a triple covalent bond / three shared pairs of electrons.
Difference: one bond in $\text{CO}$ is a dative / coordinate bond formed by donation of a lone pair from O to C, whereas all three bonds in $\text{N}_{2}$ are normal shared pairs.

hints: Add up the atomic numbers of the two atoms in each molecule to find the total electrons per molecule.
Use the electronegativity difference, 2.5 for C versus 3.5 for O and 3.0 versus 3.0 for N2, to decide which molecule is polar and which is non-polar.
walkthrough:
Count electrons like counting protons**
For a neutral molecule total electrons equals total protons. Nitrogen has atomic number 7, so $\text{N}_{2}$ has $7 + 7 = 14$ electrons. Carbon is 6 and oxygen is 8, so $\text{CO}$ has $6 + 8 = 14$ electrons. They are isoelectronic, same electron count.

Link electronegativity to polarity then to forces**
In $\text{N}_{2}$ both atoms have electronegativity 3.0, so the bond is non-polar with no permanent dipole. The only van der Waals force possible is instantaneous dipole-induced dipole. In $\text{CO}$ the difference is $3.5 - 2.5 = 1.0$, so the molecule is polar with a permanent dipole. Polar molecules still have instantaneous dipole-induced dipole forces as well, but additionally show permanent dipole-permanent dipole forces.

Final answer: Number of electrons per molecule: $\text{N}_{2}$ = 14 ; $\text{CO}$ = 14.
Type(s) of intermolecular force: $\text{N}_{2}$ = instantaneous dipole-induced dipole only ; $\text{CO}$ = permanent dipole-permanent dipole plus instantaneous dipole-induced dipole.

hints: Compare the symmetry of charge in N2 with the uneven charge distribution in CO from the electronegativity data.
walkthrough:
See why bond strength is not the whole story**
You might think the stronger bond should always be less reactive, but reactivity also depends on polarity. $\text{N}_{2}$ is completely symmetrical and non-polar, so there is no partial charge for another molecule or ion to be attracted to. $\text{CO}$ has $\delta+$ on C and $\delta-$ on O because oxygen pulls electrons more strongly, giving a permanent dipole that makes attack by other species much easier.
Final answer: $\text{CO}$ is polar / has a permanent dipole whereas $\text{N}_{2}$ is non-polar, so $\text{CO}$ can be attacked by charged species more easily.

hints: Recall the two ideal gas assumptions about negligible molecular volume and negligible intermolecular forces, and think what T and p make them most true.
walkthrough:
Make the real gas behave ideally**
An ideal gas assumes particles have negligible volume and no attractions for each other. High temperature gives particles so much kinetic energy that attractions become insignificant. Low pressure means particles are far apart, so their own volume is negligible compared with the container and collisions are rare.
Final answer: High temperature and low pressure.

hints: Recall from (a)(ii) which gas has only instantaneous dipole-induced dipole forces and which has additional permanent dipole forces.
Link stronger intermolecular forces to greater deviation from the ideal assumption of no attractions.
walkthrough:
Compare the attractions in the two gases**
You already worked out that $\text{N}_{2}$ has only weak instantaneous dipole-induced dipole forces, while polar $\text{CO}$ has permanent dipole-permanent dipole forces in addition. So attractions between $\text{CO}$ molecules are stronger.

Connect stronger attractions to less ideal behaviour**
Ideal behaviour assumes zero attraction between particles. Because $\text{CO}$ has more significant attractions, it deviates more from that assumption. $\text{N}_{2}$ with weaker, less significant forces follows the ideal model more closely at the same $20.0^{\circ}\text{C}$ and $101\text{ kPa}$.

Final answer: $\text{CO}$ is polar / has a permanent dipole whereas $\text{N}_{2}$ is non-polar.
Intermolecular forces in $\text{CO}$ are stronger / more significant than in $\text{N}_{2}$, so $\text{N}_{2}$ obeys the ideal assumption of no IMF more closely.

hints: Convert pressure to Pa, volume to $\text{m}^{3}$ and temperature to K before substituting.
Recall the governing relation $pV = nRT$ rearranged to $n = pV/RT$ with $R = 8.31 \text{ J K}^{-1} \text{ mol}^{-1}$.
Substitute your converted values and check the power of ten carefully to obtain n in mol.
walkthrough:
Convert everything to SI base units**
The gas constant $R = 8.31 \text{ J K}^{-1} \text{ mol}^{-1}$ only works if you use Pa, $\text{m}^{3}$ and K. So convert: $$p = 101 \text{ kPa} = 101 \times 1000 = 101000 \text{ Pa}$$ $$V = 100 \text{ cm}^{3} = 100/1000000 = 1.0 \times 10^{-4} \text{ m}^{3}$$ $$T = 20.0 + 273 = 293 \text{ K}$$ A common slip is using $\text{cm}^{3}$ directly, that gives an answer a million times too big.

Apply the ideal gas equation**
Rearrange $pV = nRT$ to make amount the subject: $$n = \frac{pV}{RT}$$ Now substitute: $$n = \frac{101000 \times 1.0 \times 10^{-4}}{8.31 \times 293}$$

Calculate and give the final amount**
Numerator $= 10.1$. Denominator $= 8.31 \times 293 = 2434.83$. So $$n = \frac{10.1}{2434.83} = 4.15 \times 10^{-3} \text{ mol}$$ Keep three significant figures to match the data and always include the unit mol.
